behavior_items: The testcase exercises the C++23 feature that allows a structured binding declaration to appear directly as the condition of a `while` or `for` loop. In pre-C++23 modes GCC is expected to issue only an extension/availability warning, not reject the code or crash.

Type `T` is made tuple-like by specializing `std::tuple_size<T>` to `2` and `std::tuple_element<I, T>` to `S`, and by providing `template<int I> S get()`. This causes `auto [i, j] = T{...}` to decompose a temporary `T` object into two bound names obtained through `get<0>()` and `get<1>()`.

`S` is intentionally non-trivial for lifetime management: it has user-defined constructors and a user-defined destructor. Because `get<I>()` returns `S` by value, each structured-binding element materializes as its own temporary/object needing destruction, so the decomposition introduces multiple independent cleanups.

`T` also has a user-defined destructor and an `explicit operator bool() const noexcept` that returns `a.s == b.s`. In a condition such as `while (auto [i, j] = T{1,1,3})`, the controlling expression is not based on `i` or `j`; the hidden decomposed object is contextually converted to `bool` via `T::operator bool`, which evaluates true because the first two members are initialized to equal values.

In `foo`, the loop condition creates a fresh temporary `T{1,1,3}` on each iteration, decomposes it, converts the underlying object to `bool`, enters the body, and may exit via `break` if `x` is true. This stresses cleanup generation on both the normal path leaving the body and the abrupt path leaving the loop via `break`.

In `bar`, the `for` loop uses the same structured-binding condition form together with an initializer (`int cnt = 0`) and increment (`++cnt`). The condition object `T{2,2,4}` also converts to true every time, so the loop body is entered unless terminated by `break`. This variant checks that the same condition-lifetime logic works inside `for` lowering as well as `while` lowering.

The key compiler behavior under test is scope and destruction for structured bindings in conditions. A condition declaration normally has cleanup at the end of each loop test/iteration, but with structured bindings GCC must account for the hidden decomposition object plus potentially separate bound variables, each of which may carry its own destructor cleanup.

The bug report explains the regression: GCC had an internal assumption that a loop condition contributes either no cleanup or only a single cleanup. That assumption became invalid for structured bindings used as conditions, because decomposing tuple-like `T` into `i` and `j` can produce multiple destructor actions.

As a result, during lowering or cleanup chaining for `while`/`for` conditions, GCC mis-modeled the condition declaration and hit an internal compiler error instead of merely compiling the extension and emitting the expected warning in older language modes.

The reproducer is carefully minimal but sufficient: tuple-like decomposition forces structured-binding semantics, user-defined destructors force nontrivial cleanups, `operator bool` makes the decomposed object usable as a loop condition, and the presence of `break` ensures the compiler must reason about all exits when attaching cleanups to the loop condition scope.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer targets GCC's handling of structured bindings used as loop conditions. It defines a tuple-like type `T` whose decomposition yields two non-trivial `S` objects and whose hidden condition object is converted to `bool` through `operator bool()`. Both `while` and `for` forms repeatedly create and decompose a temporary `T`, then require GCC to emit correct destruction for multiple bound objects on normal iteration and on `break`. The regression was that GCC assumed a condition had at most one cleanup, but a structured-binding condition can require several, so the compiler crashed with an ICE instead of just accepting the construct as a C++23 feature or warning about it in older modes.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: Common pattern: the failure is triggered specifically by a structured binding used as the condition of `while`/`for`, where tuple-like decomposition of a temporary produces more than one non-trivially destructible bound object. That means the condition is not a simple single-expression or single-declaration case: GCC must manage the hidden synthesized object for the condition, the per-binding objects created from `get<0>()` and `get<1>()`, contextual conversion of the underlying object to `bool`, and destruction on every exit path of the loop test scope, including `break`. The reported regression strongly suggests loop-condition lowering or C++ cleanup bookkeeping still assumes a condition contributes at most zero or one cleanup action. Structured bindings violate that assumption because each bound name can carry its own cleanup, and the hidden decomposition object may also need lifetime handling. So the most likely bug class is incorrect representation, chaining, or emission of multiple cleanups for condition declarations during C++ front-end lowering of `while`/`for` loops.
possible_causes: Bug in C++ front-end loop-condition lowering for structured bindings: code handling `while`/`for` condition declarations likely assumes a single cleanup node and ICEs when a structured binding condition produces multiple cleanups.

Incorrect cleanup chaining for structured-binding components: GCC may register only one destructor/cleanup for the condition scope, then encounter unexpected extra cleanup records for additional bound names and fail an internal consistency check.

Lifetime/scope modeling defect for hidden structured-binding temporaries in conditions: the compiler may mishandle the hidden decomposed object versus the individual bindings, especially when both require destruction before the next iteration or on `break`.

Regression in the PR86769-related implementation of P0963R3 support: newly added condition-declaration logic for structured bindings likely reuses old single-variable condition code paths that are not generalized to tuple-like decomposition.

Incorrect abrupt-exit cleanup generation from loop bodies: when the condition declaration has multiple destructible entities, the `break` path may expose missing or malformed EH/cleanup edges and trigger an ICE during gimplification or tree cleanup expansion.

Defect in tuple-like structured-binding expansion inside conditional contexts: decomposition through `tuple_size`/`tuple_element`/`get<I>()` returning by value may create separate materialized temporaries that the condition-handling code does not expect, leading to invalid tree state or duplicated/missing destructor actions.
evidence: The bug report explicitly states the broken assumption: 'there is no or just a single cleanup' is false for structured bindings used as a condition.
`S` has a user-defined destructor and `get<I>()` returns `S` by value, so each binding element can require its own destruction rather than sharing a trivial lifetime.
The condition form is used in both `while` and `for`, pointing to shared loop-condition handling rather than a bug in one specific loop syntax.
`T` is contextually converted to `bool` via `operator bool()`, so GCC must preserve the hidden condition object long enough for conversion while also managing decomposition cleanups.
The loop body contains `break`, which forces cleanup emission on an abrupt exit path and increases the chance of exposing malformed cleanup stacks or scope-exit logic.

Expected behavior in pre-C++23 modes is only a warning, but GCC instead ICEs, which is typical of an internal front-end invariant violation in scope/cleanup representation rather than semantic rejection of the source.

selected_files.reason: Most likely location for the regression because C++ loop-condition semantic lowering lives here, including construction of `while`/`for` conditions, statement scopes, and cleanup attachment. The bug report explicitly points to an invalid assumption that a condition has at most one cleanup, which fits front-end condition-building logic for structured bindings.

Structured bindings and their synthesized declarations are created and managed in the C++ declaration machinery. If each binding element in a condition can contribute its own destructor cleanup, this file is a strong suspect for mishandling or underreporting the number of cleanups associated with the structured-binding declaration.

P0963R3 support for structured bindings in conditions requires parser-side handling of declaration conditions in `while` and `for`. Since the regression is described as coming after the feature work, parser logic that routes this new syntax into older single-declaration condition code paths is suspicious.

If the front end builds the right trees but genericization/gimplification assumes a condition declaration yields only one cleanup, the ICE can occur here when lowering structured-binding conditions with multiple destructible bound names into generic or gimple form.

Core gimplification manages cleanup sequencing and scope lowering. A latent assumption in generic cleanup handling that a loop condition contributes zero or one cleanup could be exposed once the C++ front end feeds it a structured-binding condition with multiple cleanups.

Although this is shared C-family infrastructure, condition lowering and cleanup sequencing helpers here can affect how loop conditions are transformed before middle-end handling. It is a plausible place for an invariant that does not expect multiple cleanups from one condition construct.

The failure description is cleanup-centric, including destruction on normal exits and `break` paths. C++ EH/cleanup helper routines in this file are a plausible source if structured-binding condition components are wrapped or chained incorrectly as cleanups.

If the ICE appears after front-end lowering, tree-level EH/cleanup region bookkeeping is a candidate because multiple destructor actions attached to a single loop-condition scope may violate assumptions in cleanup region creation or edge wiring.

gcc/cp/decl.cc.summary: We're initializing a local variable which has a cleanup GUARD. If there are any temporaries used in the initializer INIT of this variable, we need to wrap their cleanups with TRY_CATCH_EXPR (, GUARD) so that the variable will be cleaned up properly if one of them throws. Unfortunately, there's no way to express this properly in terms of nesting, as the regions for the temporaries overlap the region for the variable itself; if there are two temporaries, the variable needs to be the first thing destroyed if either of the temporary destructors throws. However, we only want to run the variable's cleanup if it actually got constructed. So we need to guard the temporary cleanups with the variable's cleanup if they are run on the normal path, but not if they are run on the exceptional path. We implement this by telling honor_protect_cleanup_actions to strip the variable cleanup from the exceptional path. Another approach could be to make the variable cleanup region enclose initialization, but depend on a flag to indicate that the variable is initialized; that's effectively what we do for arrays. But the current approach works fine for non-arrays, and has no code overhead in the usual case

Do the same if the current function might use the named return value optimization, so we don't destroy it on return. Otherwise, returns NULL_TREE.
